shortQuestions: Organic compounds are the compounds of carbon (chiefly with hydrogen, and also with O, N, S, P and halogens), i.e. hydrocarbons and their derivatives — excluding simple carbon compounds such as oxides of carbon, carbonates and cyanides.
Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the study of hydrocarbons and their derivatives.

Lassaigne's test: fuse a small piece of sodium with the organic compound in an ignition tube; plunge the red-hot tube into distilled water, boil and filter. The filtrate is the sodium (Lassaigne's) extract. Na + C + N → NaCN.
Boil part of the extract with freshly prepared FeSO₄ solution, cool, add a few drops of FeCl₃ and acidify with dilute H₂SO₄.
A Prussian blue colour or precipitate shows nitrogen: 6NaCN + FeSO₄ → Na₄[Fe(CN)₆] + Na₂SO₄; 3Na₄[Fe(CN)₆] + 4FeCl₃ → Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃ (Prussian blue) + 12NaCl.
A homologous series is a group of organic compounds with the same functional group in which each member differs from the next by a –CH₂– group.

Characteristics: all members have the same general formula (e.g. alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂); they have similar chemical properties; their physical properties (boiling point, density) change gradually with molecular mass; they can be prepared by similar general methods; successive molecular masses differ by 14.
Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) is an allotrope of carbon, but its molecule is a closed cage of fused five- and six-membered carbon rings with alternating double bonds, rather like aromatic compounds.

It behaves like an organic molecule: it dissolves in organic solvents and undergoes organic reactions (addition, hydrogenation, halogenation) forming many derivatives. So it is studied in organic chemistry.
Carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide (CO₂).

Carbonates and hydrogencarbonates (CaCO₃, NaHCO₃), carbides (CaC₂, SiC), cyanides and cyanates (KCN, KCNO), hydrogen cyanide, carbonic acid and metal carbonyls. These are studied in inorganic chemistry.

Partial synthesis: preparing a compound starting from a naturally occurring compound that already has much of the required structure, e.g. semi-synthetic penicillins made from natural penicillin, or vitamin preparations from natural steroids.
Total synthesis: preparing a compound entirely from simple starting materials (ultimately from the elements), e.g. Wöhler's synthesis of urea and Kolbe's synthesis of acetic acid.
Fischer–Tropsch process: coal (coke) is heated with steam to give water gas, C + H₂O → CO + H₂.

Water gas, enriched with hydrogen, is passed over an iron or cobalt catalyst at about 200–300 °C and a few atmospheres: nCO + (2n + 1)H₂ → CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + nH₂O, giving a mixture of hydrocarbons (synthetic petrol).
(Bergius process: powdered coal is hydrogenated directly with H₂ at high pressure over a catalyst.)
Catenation: carbon atoms link with one another to form long chains, branched chains and rings of almost any size.
Tetravalency: each carbon forms four strong covalent bonds, including double and triple bonds.
Carbon bonds strongly with H, O, N, S, P and halogens.
Isomerism: the same molecular formula can give many different structures. Together these give millions of organic compounds.
Acyclic (open-chain or aliphatic) compounds have carbon atoms joined in straight or branched chains with no ring, e.g. butane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, isobutane.

Cyclic (closed-chain) compounds have atoms joined in rings: homocyclic rings contain only carbon (alicyclic, e.g. cyclohexane; aromatic, e.g. benzene) and heterocyclic rings contain another atom (e.g. pyridine, furan).
longQuestions: Fossil fuels are fuels formed from the remains of plants and animals buried for millions of years under high temperature and pressure without air. They are coal, petroleum and natural gas.

Coal: a black solid formed from plant remains; types (rank) by increasing carbon content — peat (≈ 60%), lignite (≈ 70%), bituminous (≈ 80%) and anthracite (≈ 90%). Used as fuel and, by destructive distillation, as a source of coke, coal gas and coal tar.

Petroleum (crude oil): a dark viscous liquid mixture of mainly saturated hydrocarbons, found trapped in porous rocks. It is refined by fractional distillation into refinery gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oils, paraffin wax and bitumen.
Natural gas: mainly methane (with ethane, propane, butane), found above petroleum deposits or alone; a clean fuel for homes, industry and vehicles (CNG) and a raw material for fertilisers.
Fossil fuels are non-renewable, and their burning releases CO₂ and pollutants.
Carbon and hydrogen: heat the compound with dry copper(II) oxide. Carbon is oxidised to CO₂, which turns lime water milky; hydrogen forms H₂O, which turns white anhydrous CuSO₄ blue.
Nitrogen, sulphur and halogens — Lassaigne's test: fuse with sodium to convert them into NaCN, Na₂S and NaX, then dissolve in water (sodium extract).

Nitrogen: boil with FeSO₄, add FeCl₃ and acidify — Prussian blue colour. Sulphur: add sodium nitroprusside — violet colour; or add lead acetate and acetic acid — black precipitate of PbS. Nitrogen and sulphur together give NaSCN, which gives a blood-red colour with FeCl₃.
Halogens: acidify with dilute HNO₃, boil off HCN and H₂S, add AgNO₃ — white AgCl (soluble in NH₄OH) shows chlorine, pale yellow AgBr (sparingly soluble) bromine, yellow AgI (insoluble) iodine.
Oxygen has no direct test; its percentage is found by difference.
Destructive distillation: coal is heated strongly (about 1000 °C) in the absence of air; it decomposes into four main fractions.
Coal gas (H₂, CH₄, CO and others): used as a fuel for heating and lighting.
Ammoniacal liquor (aqueous ammonia and ammonium salts): treated with H₂SO₄ to give ammonium sulphate fertiliser.

Coal tar: a thick black liquid; fractional distillation gives benzene, toluene, phenol, naphthalene, anthracene and pitch — raw materials for dyes, drugs, explosives, plastics, perfumes and insecticides; pitch is used for road surfacing and roofing.
Coke (residue, nearly pure carbon): a smokeless fuel and a reducing agent in the extraction of iron; used to make water gas and producer gas.
Organic compounds are covalent; most do not ionise and are non-electrolytes.
They usually have low melting and boiling points; many are volatile liquids or gases.
Most are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents (alcohol, ether, benzene); many are combustible, burning to CO₂ and H₂O.
Their reactions are generally slow, involve molecules and often need heat or catalysts, giving side products.
Catenation and isomerism are common, so there is an enormous number of organic compounds; they show homologous series with similar properties.
A functional group is an atom or group of atoms in a molecule that is responsible for its characteristic chemical properties.

Classes by functional group: alkenes (C=C), alkynes (C≡C), alkyl halides (–X), alcohols (–OH), ethers (R–O–R), aldehydes (–CHO), ketones (>C=O), carboxylic acids (–COOH), esters (–COOR), amines (–NH₂), amides (–CONH₂), nitriles (–C≡N), nitro compounds (–NO₂), acid halides (–COX), acid anhydrides.
Examples: CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol, alcohol), CH₃CHO (ethanal, aldehyde), CH₃COCH₃ (propanone, ketone), CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid), CH₃NH₂ (methylamine).
All compounds with the same functional group form a homologous series and react in similar ways.
Organic compounds are classified by the arrangement of carbon atoms into open-chain and closed-chain compounds.
Open-chain (acyclic or aliphatic) compounds: carbon atoms form straight chains (n-butane) or branched chains (isobutane); they may be saturated or unsaturated.

Closed-chain (cyclic) compounds: (i) Homocyclic (carbocyclic) — rings contain only carbon atoms: alicyclic compounds (cyclopropane, cyclohexane) and aromatic compounds (benzene, naphthalene). (ii) Heterocyclic — rings containing one or more other atoms such as N, O or S (pyridine, furan, thiophene).
activities: Carbon and hydrogen: mix a little dry urea with dry copper(II) oxide in a hard-glass test tube and heat. Pass the gas into lime water — it turns milky (CO₂), so carbon is present. Droplets on the cooler part of the tube turn white anhydrous CuSO₄ blue (H₂O), so hydrogen is present.

Nitrogen: fuse urea with a small piece of sodium (Lassaigne's test), dissolve in water and filter. Boil the filtrate with FeSO₄ solution, add a few drops of FeCl₃ and acidify with dilute H₂SO₄ — a Prussian blue colour confirms nitrogen.
(Quick check: warming urea with NaOH solution gives ammonia, which turns moist red litmus blue.)
